stops.name: Route 66 Begin Sign
stops.blurb: East Adams Street, where the Mother Road officially starts. The sign moved a few times over the decades; the current one faces west toward 2,448 miles of road.

stops.name: Lou Mitchell's
stops.blurb: Serving breakfast since 1923, three years before the highway existed. Traditional first stop before heading west.

stops.name: Henry's Drive-In
stops.blurb: A working hot-dog stand on the Cicero alignment with a surviving Muffler Man out front. Most westbound trips skip it between Chicago and Wilmington.

stops.name: Dell Rhea's Chicken Basket
stops.blurb: 1946 roadhouse on the National Register. Fried chicken in a basket, corn fritters, and a neon sign that still works. The dining room has been feeding 66 travelers since before the interstate.

stops.name: Joliet Area Historical Museum
stops.blurb: Route 66 gallery in a converted church, plus some of the best early bridges on the Illinois stretch. Most people leave Chicago and don't stop until Wilmington.

stops.name: Gemini Giant
stops.blurb: A fiberglass spaceman holding a rocket, one of the surviving Muffler Man giants. Relocated within town in recent years — check current siting.

stops.name: Polk-a-Dot Drive In
stops.blurb: 1950s drive-in with statues of Elvis, Marilyn and the Blues Brothers out front. Still a working burger joint, not a museum piece.

stops.name: Gardner Two-Cell Jail
stops.blurb: An 1906 two-cell calaboose the size of a garden shed, beside a relocated 1930s streetcar diner. Both free, both usually deserted.

stops.name: Ambler's Texaco Gas Station
stops.blurb: 1933 cottage-style station that pumped fuel for 66 years — one of the longest operating runs on the route. Restored, now a visitor center.

stops.name: Standard Oil Gas Station
stops.blurb: 1932 domestic-style station saved by a local preservation grant. Small, precise, and usually empty of crowds.

stops.name: Meramec Caverns Barn
stops.blurb: One of the last surviving painted barn advertisements from the campaign that made Meramec Caverns famous. Roadside, no facilities.

stops.name: Route 66 Hall of Fame & Museum
stops.blurb: Housed in the old fire station, plus a wall-sized mural out back that has become the town's photo spot.

stops.name: Sprague's Super Service
stops.blurb: A 1931 Tudor Revival station and cafe with an apartment above it, restored and run as a gift shop and information stop. Lit at night and worth seeing even when closed.

stops.name: Dixie Truckers Home
stops.blurb: Opened 1928 in a mechanic's garage with six stools. Claims the title of oldest continuously operating truck stop in the country.

stops.name: Funks Grove Pure Maple Sirup
stops.blurb: Family-run since the 1820s. Spelled 'sirup' deliberately — it means no sugar added. Sells out most seasons.

stops.name: The Shake Shack
stops.blurb: No relation to the chain. A small-town burger and malt counter that long predates it.

stops.name: Palms Grill Cafe
stops.blurb: 1934 cafe restored to period, down to the bus-flag system for flagging down Greyhounds. Pie is the reason to stop.

stops.name: Bunyon Giant
stops.blurb: A Paul Bunyan giant holding a hot dog instead of an axe. Moved here from Cicero when its original stand closed.

stops.name: American Giants Museum
stops.blurb: A restored station with cement pads where damaged or orphaned Muffler Men from across the country are collected and displayed. Atlanta has four giants in town and room for more.
stops.caution: Small town, limited hours — check before detouring.

stops.name: Railsplitter Covered Wagon
stops.blurb: A giant covered wagon driven by a fiberglass Abraham Lincoln reading a book. Held a world record for a while.

stops.name: The Mill Museum on Route 66
stops.blurb: A restored 1929 Dutch mill restaurant, now a small Route 66 museum on the Lincoln alignment. Easy to miss next to the covered-wagon giant.

stops.name: Shea's Gas Station
stops.blurb: Bill Shea's packed 1950s station museum — pumps, porcelain, and signs stacked to the rafters. Hours are irregular; Wednesday is the usual bet.
stops.caution: Irregular hours — check before detouring.

stops.name: Lincoln's Tomb
stops.blurb: Oak Ridge Cemetery. The route runs along the edge of it.

stops.name: Cozy Dog Drive In
stops.blurb: Where the corn dog on a stick was popularized in 1946. Run by the Waldmire family, whose Route 66 map art you'll see all the way to California.

stops.name: Ace Sign Museum
stops.blurb: A working fifth-generation sign shop that saved 85-plus neon and porcelain Route 66 signs inside a 1952 Sears warehouse. Tours on weekdays. High ratings, still under-visited.
stops.caution: Weekday tours; call ahead on weekends.

stops.name: Route 66 Drive In
stops.blurb: 1951 screen, still showing double features from spring through autumn.

stops.name: Motorheads Bar & Grill
stops.blurb: A large complex of restored cars, Route 66 signage and live music, with its own giant out front holding the sign.

stops.name: Illinois Brick Road
stops.blurb: About a mile and a half of original 1926–1930 brick pavement still in use. One of the last surviving brick stretches of the highway. Drive it slowly.
stops.caution: Narrow original brick — watch for farm traffic.

stops.name: Soulsby Service Station
stops.blurb: A 1926 Shell station built the same year as the highway and run by the same family until 1991. Restored by volunteers.

stops.name: Mother Jones Monument
stops.blurb: Mary Harris Jones asked to be buried with the miners killed in the 1898 Virden riots. The Union Miners Cemetery is the only union-owned cemetery in the country and sits a minute off the road.

stops.name: Sky View Drive-In
stops.blurb: 1950 drive-in theater, still projecting. The last operating drive-in on Illinois 66.

stops.name: Litchfield Museum & Welcome Center
stops.blurb: Small, free, and the best place in Illinois to work out which alignment you're actually driving.

stops.name: Ariston Cafe
stops.blurb: Open since 1924 and on the National Register. One of the oldest continuously running restaurants on the route.

stops.name: Pink Elephant Antique Mall
stops.blurb: A converted school fronted by a pink fiberglass elephant, a Muffler Man and a full-size Futuro house.

stops.name: Henry's Rabbit Ranch
stops.blurb: A visitor center, a row of buried Volkswagen Rabbits parodying Cadillac Ranch, and actual rabbits.

stops.name: It's Electric Neon Sign Park
stops.blurb: A new outdoor park of restored neon on the approach to the Mississippi. Best after dark, a few miles before Chain of Rocks.

stops.name: Chain of Rocks Bridge
stops.blurb: The old Mississippi crossing with a 22-degree bend mid-span. Pedestrian and bike only now — walk to the kink and look down.

stops.name: Gateway Arch
stops.blurb: Not a Route 66 site, but unavoidable and worth the tram to the top.

stops.name: Crown Candy Kitchen
stops.blurb: Open since 1913. Malts, hand-dipped chocolate, and a BLT that St. Louis treats as a civic monument. A few minutes north of the Arch in Old North.
stops.caution: Closed Sundays. Small room — go early.

stops.name: Ted Drewes Frozen Custard
stops.blurb: On the Chippewa alignment since 1941. Order a concrete; they hand it to you upside down.

stops.name: Lone Elk Park
stops.blurb: A drive-through county park next to Route 66 State Park where elk and bison range around the car.
stops.caution: No pets, even inside a closed vehicle.

stops.name: Route 66 State Park
stops.blurb: Built on the site of Times Beach, a town evacuated and demolished after dioxin contamination in the 1980s. The visitor center is the old roadhouse.

stops.name: Campbell's Service Museum
stops.blurb: A restored 1930s service station west of Route 66 State Park, now a compact museum of pumps and period tools.

stops.name: Red Cedar Inn
stops.blurb: 1934 Ozark-cedar roadhouse on the National Register. The dining room is a museum now, but the building is the point.

stops.name: Meramec Caverns
stops.blurb: The cave that invented the barn-roof billboard. Commercial, crowded, and historically central to roadside advertising.

stops.name: Bourbon Water Tower
stops.blurb: A water tower that says BOURBON in enormous letters. That's the whole attraction and it works.

stops.name: Wagon Wheel Motel
stops.blurb: 1930s stone cottages, continuously operating, restored rather than themed. One of the best places to actually sleep on the route.

stops.name: World's Largest Rocking Chair
stops.blurb: Forty-two feet of welded steel outside a general store. No longer holds the world record, still enormous.

stops.name: Mule Trading Post
stops.blurb: Hillbilly-kitsch souvenir stand that has been luring cars off the road since the 1940s. The neon mule is the draw.

stops.name: John's Modern Cabins
stops.blurb: Six collapsing 1930s tourist cabins in the trees beside an abandoned alignment. Unsigned, unstaffed, slowly losing to the weather.

stops.name: Trail of Tears Monument
stops.blurb: Larry Baggett's handmade memorial on the old alignment near the Gasconade. Easy to miss if you stay on I-44.

stops.name: Hooker Cut
stops.blurb: A deep rock cut blasted in 1943, one of the first four-lane divided stretches of highway in the country. Built to move military traffic to Fort Leonard Wood.

stops.name: Devil's Elbow Bridge
stops.blurb: 1923 truss bridge over the Big Piney on a bypassed alignment through the Ozarks. Almost nobody stops here and they should.

stops.name: Elbow Inn
stops.blurb: A roadhouse across the bridge, decorated in a way that surprises first-time visitors. Been serving since the 1930s.

stops.name: Uranus Fudge Factory
stops.blurb: A general store that has built an entire business on one joke and commits to it completely. Also home to a very large belt buckle.

stops.name: Neon Sign Park
stops.blurb: Restored motel and cafe neon clustered on the St. Robert alignment. Worth a slow pass after sunset.

stops.name: Munger Moss Motel
stops.blurb: Neon sign from 1955, still lit, still taking bookings. Ask about the themed rooms.

stops.name: Birthplace of Route 66 Roadside Park
stops.blurb: Springfield is where the highway got its number in 1926, by telegram. A small park marks it.

stops.name: Gillioz Theatre
stops.blurb: 1926 theatre restored to working order, now hosting films and touring acts. Easy to walk past without realising what it is.

stops.name: Rail Haven Motel
stops.blurb: A 1938 stone motor court now operating under a chain flag but with its original neon kept intact.

stops.name: Route 66 Car Museum
stops.blurb: Dozens of vintage cars in a Springfield warehouse a few blocks off the square. A serious collection that most through-trips skip.

stops.name: Rest Haven Court
stops.blurb: 1947 motor court with original neon, still renting rooms.

stops.name: Halltown
stops.blurb: Once called Little Chicago for its density of businesses. Now a row of leaning storefronts on the old alignment.

stops.name: Gay Parita Sinclair Station
stops.blurb: A meticulous 1930 station recreation built by hand. Family-run since the founder's death; hours are informal.

stops.name: Spencer Station
stops.blurb: An entire 1920s block — barbershop, store, cafe, filling station — bought by one couple in 2022 and being restored to its 1930s and 40s look. Designated a Route 66 Roadside Attraction in 2023.

stops.name: Avilla
stops.blurb: Part of southwest Missouri's Ghost Stretch. A handful of derelict buildings and almost no traffic.

stops.name: Kellogg Lake Park
stops.blurb: The lake is a 1953 borrow pit dug to build the new alignment. Original 66 pavement runs along the Spring River on the east side, the 1950s alignment borders the west. Free, with a fountain, disc golf and a pavilion.

stops.name: Red Oak II
stops.blurb: An artist moved an entire abandoned village here building by building and rebuilt it as a sculpture. Genuinely strange and mostly deserted.

stops.name: Pancake Hut
stops.blurb: Breakfast counter with a working Chicago Coin Band Box — an animatronic big-band machine, one of very few left anywhere. It plays while you eat and nothing outside advertises it.

stops.name: Boots Court Motel
stops.blurb: Streamline Moderne, restored to its 1949 appearance including radio-only rooms. Clark Gable reportedly stayed here.

stops.name: 66 Drive-In Theatre
stops.blurb: 1949 screen, restored and operating seasonally. On the National Register.

stops.name: SuperTam Superman Museum
stops.blurb: An ice cream parlor stuffed with decades of Superman memorabilia, right on the Webb City alignment. Closed Sundays and Mondays.
stops.caution: Closed Sunday and Monday.

stops.name: Cars on the Route
stops.blurb: The 1934 Kan-O-Tex station, now a shop, with the rusty tow truck that inspired a Pixar character parked outside.

stops.name: Rainbow Curve Bridge
stops.blurb: The last surviving Marsh Arch 'rainbow' bridge on Route 66. Single lane, 1923, easy to miss.

stops.name: Nelson's Old Riverton Store
stops.blurb: A 1925 general store still selling groceries and sandwiches to the same community it always has.

stops.name: Baxter Springs Independent Oil Station
stops.blurb: A 1930 cottage-style station restored as the town's Route 66 visitor centre. Kansas only has thirteen miles of highway; this is one of its best buildings.

stops.name: Dairy King
stops.blurb: Burgers and Route 66-shaped cookies out of a former filling station. Cash only.

stops.name: Mickey Mantle Boyhood Home
stops.blurb: A small clapboard house with the barn siding he hit balls against. Privately owned; view from the street.

stops.name: Coleman Theatre
stops.blurb: A 1929 Spanish Colonial Revival cinema with its original Wurlitzer. Free tours, largely unvisited.

stops.name: Ribbon Road (Sidewalk Highway)
stops.blurb: Six and a half miles of nine-foot-wide concrete laid in 1922, four years before the highway existed. Two cars cannot pass. Gravel in places; drive it slowly.

stops.name: Afton Station
stops.blurb: A restored 1930s DX station housing a Packard collection, run on volunteer hours.

stops.name: Little Cabin Creek Iron Bridge
stops.blurb: A surviving iron truss on an early Oklahoma alignment east of Vinita. One-lane, original, and almost always empty.
stops.caution: One-lane historic bridge — walk it if you prefer.

stops.name: Clanton's Cafe
stops.blurb: Family-run since 1927 and one of the oldest continuously operating restaurants on the Oklahoma stretch. Chicken-fried steak is the order.

stops.name: Blue Whale of Catoosa
stops.blurb: Built in the early 1970s as an anniversary gift for the builder's wife. Free, weird, and beloved.

stops.name: Pryor Creek Bridge
stops.blurb: A 1926 steel truss on the original 66 alignment through Chelsea. Photogenic and usually deserted.

stops.name: Totem Pole Park
stops.blurb: Ed Galloway spent 1937 to 1948 building a ninety-foot concrete totem pole and a fiddle house around it. Free, and one of the great American folk-art sites.

stops.name: Andy Payne Memorial
stops.blurb: Payne won the 1928 Trans-American Footrace from Los Angeles to New York — 84 days of running, beating second place by more than fifteen hours. His hometown marks it and almost nobody stops.

stops.name: Will Rogers Memorial Museum
stops.blurb: The highway was named for him. Substantial collection, quiet weekdays.

stops.name: Meadow Gold Sign
stops.blurb: A 1930s dairy sign saved from demolition and remounted on a purpose-built pavilion. Best after dark.

stops.name: Golden Driller
stops.blurb: A 76-foot oilman, the official state monument of Oklahoma, standing at the fairgrounds.

stops.name: Cyrus Avery Centennial Plaza
stops.blurb: Sculptures of the Avery family in a Model T at the 11th Street Bridge, where the man who argued for Route 66 is honored in his own city.

stops.name: Route 66 Neon Sign Park
stops.blurb: Restored Tulsa neon — Meadow Gold's neighbors — clustered at the west end of 11th Street. Best after dark.

stops.name: Buck Atom's Cosmic Curios
stops.blurb: A space-cowboy Muffler Man outside a souvenir shop on the Tulsa stretch. Recent, but a genuine addition to the road.

stops.name: Rock Creek Bridge
stops.blurb: A 1921 truss bridge with a brick deck on a bypassed alignment. Low clearance — under seven foot two.

stops.name: Heart of Route 66 Auto Museum
stops.blurb: Cars, pumps and a 66-foot neon soda bottle you can see from the alignment. Sapulpa's serious museum stop.

stops.name: Depew Main Street
stops.blurb: The first town Route 66 bypassed. A brick main street and the Gimmel station survive with a few hundred residents.

stops.name: Rock Cafe
stops.blurb: Built in 1939 from stone excavated during the highway's construction. Rebuilt after a 2008 fire using the original walls.

stops.name: Ozark Trail Obelisk
stops.blurb: A twenty-one-foot stone marker from the pre-highway Ozark Trail system, standing on a gravel road on a triangle of land. Graffitied and still impressive.

stops.name: Chandler Route 66 Interpretive Center
stops.blurb: Inside a 1937 armoury. Exhibits are watched from car seats and cots, which is a better idea than it sounds.

stops.name: Westfall Phillips 66 Station
stops.blurb: A restored cottage-style Phillips 66 on Chandler's original alignment, a block from the interpretive center and easy to roll past.

stops.name: Seaba Station Motorcycle Museum
stops.blurb: A 1921 filling station and machine shop, now full of vintage motorcycles and engines.

stops.name: Threatt Filling Station
stops.blurb: Built in 1915 by a Black farming family and one of very few Black-owned businesses serving travellers on segregated Route 66. Under restoration.

stops.name: Round Barn
stops.blurb: 1898 barn, genuinely round, restored by retired volunteers after its roof collapsed. Go upstairs for the acoustics.

stops.name: POPS 66 Soda Ranch
stops.blurb: A 66-foot LED soda bottle and several hundred varieties of pop. Modern, but a good stop.

stops.name: Milk Bottle Grocery
stops.blurb: A triangular 1930 building with a giant milk bottle on the roof, occupying a lot barely wider than a car.

stops.name: Tower Theatre
stops.blurb: 1937 Art Deco movie palace on Uptown 23rd. The neon marquee is the shot even if you never go inside.

stops.name: Robots on 66 (RT-19)
stops.blurb: Eight-foot tin-toy robot across from Tower Theatre. Welcome Humans. Part of Mary Beth Babcock's Robots on 66 series.

stops.name: Lake Overholser Bridge
stops.blurb: The original Route 66 crossing at the east end of the lake. National Register. Most traffic now uses the newer span.

stops.name: Route 66 Park
stops.blurb: 148 acres on Lake Overholser with a walkable map of 66, ponds, and the Cyrus Avery observation tower. Free.

stops.name: Yukon's Best Flour
stops.blurb: Grain elevators on Main Street / 66. The lighted Yukon's Best Flour sign is the west-OKC skyline. Exterior only.

stops.name: Robert's Grill
stops.blurb: Opened 1926 — same year as Route 66. Tiny counter, onion burgers smashed on the griddle. El Reno's oldest.

stops.name: Bridgeport Hill Service Station
stops.blurb: A lonely restored station on the climb west of the Canadian River, on the pre-interstate alignment most GPS units skip.

stops.name: Lucille's Service Station
stops.blurb: 1929 station and upstairs residence run by 'the Mother of the Mother Road' for nearly 60 years. Exterior only.

stops.name: Lucille's Roadhouse
stops.blurb: A 1940s-styled diner named for Lucille Hamons of Hydro. Separate from her original station.

stops.name: Stafford Air & Space Museum
stops.blurb: Smithsonian-affiliated museum for Weatherford's Thomas Stafford — his flown Apollo 10 suit and the Gemini 6A capsule under one roof.

stops.name: Oklahoma Route 66 Museum
stops.blurb: State-run, organized decade by decade. The best straight history museum on the route.

stops.name: Foss (Kobel's Station)
stops.blurb: A town rebuilt uphill after a flood, then emptied when the interstate bypassed it. A collapsed station, an 1894 church, and a jail are most of what remains.
stops.caution: Ghost-town remnants. Stay off interiors and private property.

stops.name: Canute Historic Jail
stops.blurb: A tiny territorial jail on the Canute alignment, next to the bones of the Cotton Boll Motel. Five minutes, no crowds.

stops.name: National Route 66 Museum
stops.blurb: Part of a four-museum complex including a transportation and farm museum. Larger than Clinton's.

stops.name: Beckham County Courthouse
stops.blurb: The 1911 domed courthouse the Joads rattle past in the 1940 Grapes of Wrath film. Still the center of Sayre.

stops.name: Sandhills Curiosity Shop
stops.blurb: A junk-filled former meat market whose owner performs for visitors. Hours entirely depend on whether he's home.

stops.name: 100th Meridian Museum
stops.blurb: Sits in the old Roger Miller Museum storefront, at the corner of Roger Miller and Sheb Wooley — Erick's two country-music sons.
stops.caution: Small-town hours — call ahead.

stops.name: West Winds Motel
stops.blurb: A 1948 Mission Revival motor court on the National Register. U-shaped courtyard from the years when Erick's motels filled every night.

stops.name: Texola
stops.blurb: The last town in Oklahoma. An abandoned jail, empty houses, and a bar with a painted slogan about there being no other place like it.

stops.name: U-Drop Inn / Tower Station
stops.blurb: 1936 Art Deco station in green and gold terracotta, restored and lit at night. The most photogenic building on the route.

stops.name: Devil's Rope Museum
stops.blurb: A museum devoted entirely to barbed wire, with a Route 66 collection attached. Free, genuinely interesting, almost never busy.

stops.name: 1929 Route 66 Gas Station
stops.blurb: A restored 1929 cottage station on McLean's main street, a block from the Devil's Rope Museum.

stops.name: Dirt 66 (pre-1935 alignment)
stops.blurb: A three-mile unpaved remnant of the original roadbed. Genuinely what the highway was before paving.
stops.caution: Unpaved and rutted. High-clearance vehicle only — low cars get stranded here.

stops.name: Alanreed & Jericho Gap
stops.blurb: The 66 Super Service Station and the approach to the Jericho Gap, a stretch of black clay that trapped cars for days after rain.

stops.name: Old Town Jericho
stops.blurb: What is left of Jericho, a 66 town the interstate erased. Foundations, a quiet road, and the feel of the Gap. Slightly off the later pavement.
stops.caution: Ghost town remnants — stay off private property.

stops.name: Leaning Water Tower
stops.blurb: Deliberately tilted to pull cars off the highway toward a truck stop that no longer exists. The tower stayed.

stops.name: Cross of Our Lord Jesus Christ
stops.blurb: A 190-foot stainless steel cross visible for twenty miles across the Panhandle, with a Stations of the Cross walk at its base.

stops.name: Slug Bug Ranch
stops.blurb: Five Volkswagen Beetles buried nose-down, built as a parody of Cadillac Ranch. Far more decayed and far emptier.

stops.name: Second Amendment Cowboy
stops.blurb: A repainted Muffler Man in a cowboy hat, standing near Cadillac Ranch beside a derelict RV museum. Most people photograph the Cadillacs and drive past him.

stops.name: Cadillac Ranch
stops.blurb: Ten Cadillacs nose-down in a field since 1974. Bring spray paint; repainting them is the point.

stops.name: Sixth Street Historic District
stops.blurb: Thirteen blocks of the original alignment through Amarillo, now bars, curio shops and live music. Better than the interstate attractions on either side of it.

stops.name: Golden Light Cafe & Cantina
stops.blurb: Opened in 1946 as a hamburger stand and never moved. Oldest restaurant on 66 still serving from its original building.
stops.caution: Closed Sundays.

stops.name: Big Texan Steak Ranch
stops.blurb: Home of the free 72-ounce steak if you finish it in an hour. Moved from the original 66 alignment to the interstate in 1970.

stops.name: Magnolia Station
stops.blurb: A restored 1924 station that predates the highway. Vega also has a good stretch of original brick alignment.

stops.name: Dot's Mini Museum
stops.blurb: Dot Leavitt's yard of 66 souvenirs, mostly outdoors, still standing after she passed. Informal, weathered, and free.
stops.caution: Outdoor display — hours and access vary.

stops.name: Midpoint Cafe
stops.blurb: 1,139 miles to Chicago, 1,139 to Los Angeles. The sign across the road marks the exact middle.

stops.name: Bent Door Cafe
stops.blurb: A 1948 diner built with salvaged WWII control-tower windows, bent into the doorway that named it. Closed since 1972, slowly being restored.
stops.caution: Under restoration — exterior viewing only.

stops.name: Glenrio Historic District
stops.blurb: Straddling the state line, with seventeen abandoned buildings including an Art Moderne Texaco and diner. Scenes from The Grapes of Wrath were shot here.

stops.name: Endee
stops.blurb: Ruins on the first miles inside New Mexico. Adobe walls, a collapsed motel, nothing else.

stops.name: World's Largest Flip Flop
stops.blurb: A giant sandal and gift shop in a town most through-trips never enter. Exactly the kind of roadside joke 66 was built for.

stops.name: Route 66 Monument
stops.blurb: A steel sculpture of a 1950s car fin. Best photographed at sunset with the motel neon coming on behind it.

stops.name: Tee Pee Curios
stops.blurb: A former grocery and gas station reduced to a curio shop when the highway was widened. The neon is original.

stops.name: Blue Swallow Motel
stops.blurb: 1939 motor court with garages beside each room and one of the finest surviving neon signs anywhere. Book ahead.

stops.name: Motel Safari
stops.blurb: 1959 motor lodge, restored, with a camel on the sign. Second-best neon in a town that runs on neon.

stops.name: La Cita Restaurant
stops.blurb: A concrete sombrero over a Mexican restaurant, standing since 1961.

stops.name: Montoya
stops.blurb: Richardson's Store, a 1936 bridge just east of town, and an old cemetery. Ruins only.

stops.name: Newkirk
stops.blurb: An abandoned garage and a few structures on a frontage alignment. Blink and you're past it.

stops.name: Cuervo
stops.blurb: Split in two by Interstate 40. Two churches, two schools and a filling station stand in various stages of collapse.

stops.name: Blue Hole
stops.blurb: An 80-foot artesian sinkhole at a constant 62°F, clear enough that scuba classes train in it. In the middle of the desert.

stops.name: Route 66 Auto Museum
stops.blurb: A working hot-rod shop with a museum attached. More authentic than most.

stops.name: Clines Corners
stops.blurb: A 1934 gas stop that grew into a 30,000-square-foot trading post at a lonely junction. New Mexico's largest gift shop on 66.

stops.name: Pecos National Historical Park
stops.blurb: Pueblo ruins and a Spanish mission church on the pre-1937 Santa Fe alignment. A short hike, rarely crowded, and skipped entirely by anyone taking the later route.

stops.name: La Bajada Hill
stops.blurb: The 1926–37 alignment climbed a basalt escarpment on twenty-three switchbacks. The old roadbed is still visible and walkable. Most travellers never learn it existed.

stops.name: Route 66 Musical Road
stops.blurb: Rumble strips that play America the Beautiful through the tires — eastbound, 45 mph, right wheels on the line.
stops.caution: Unmarked since 2020. Eastbound only, 45 mph, right tires on the rumble strip.

stops.name: 66 Diner
stops.blurb: A former Phillips 66 station converted to an Art Deco diner on Central Avenue.

stops.name: Nob Hill neon, Central Avenue
stops.blurb: Eighteen miles of Central Avenue were Route 66. The Nob Hill stretch keeps the densest concentration of surviving signs.

stops.name: KiMo Theatre
stops.blurb: 1927 Pueblo Deco cinema on Central Avenue, restored. Ceiling beams cast from real logs, buffalo-skull sconces.

stops.name: Dog House Drive In
stops.blurb: A 1950s chili-dog stand under one of the best surviving neon dachshunds on Central Avenue. Eat in the lot.

stops.name: El Vado Motel
stops.blurb: 1937 adobe court saved from demolition and reopened as a hotel and food hall. A rare successful adaptive reuse.

stops.name: San José de la Laguna Mission
stops.blurb: A 1699 adobe mission on the pueblo, directly above the highway. Respect posted rules on photography.

stops.name: Budville Trading Company
stops.blurb: Abandoned service station and store. A 1994 death ended 66 years in the same family. One of the most photographed ruins on New Mexico 66.
stops.caution: Private property — photograph from the roadside.

stops.name: Villa de Cubero
stops.blurb: A tourist court where Hemingway is said to have stayed while writing. Now a shuttered trading post and a row of empty cabins.

stops.name: Acoma Curio Shop
stops.blurb: A 1937 curio shop and the faded Whiting Brothers arrow across the road. What's left of a travel complex that burned in the 1990s.
stops.caution: Ruins — stay off interiors.

stops.name: Route 66 Neon Drive-Thru
stops.blurb: A neon arch you can actually drive through, built for the highway's later revival.

stops.name: New Mexico Mining Museum
stops.blurb: Built around a simulated uranium mine you descend into. Odd, specific, and the only one of its kind.

stops.name: Bowlin's Old Crater Trading Post
stops.blurb: A 1954 trading post from a trader who had worked with local Navajo families since 1912. Empty now beside the old alignment.

stops.name: Continental Divide
stops.blurb: 7,295 feet, the highest point on Route 66, marked by a trading post and not much else.

stops.name: El Rancho Hotel
stops.blurb: Built in 1936 to house film crews shooting Westerns nearby. The lobby is a two-story log-and-balcony set piece.

stops.name: Chief Yellowhorse
stops.blurb: The Hole-in-the-Wall trading post against the red sandstone at the Arizona line. A family-run stop since the 1950s, flagged as a don't-skip on detailed 66 maps.

stops.name: Lupton
stops.blurb: First stop inside Arizona, tucked under red cliffs at around 5,900 feet. Trading posts survive at the base of the rock.

stops.name: Fort Courage
stops.blurb: A mock frontier fort built to trade on a 1960s television series. Mostly abandoned now.

stops.name: Painted Desert Trading Post
stops.blurb: A lone adobe building on a dirt alignment miles from pavement, with hand-painted lettering still faintly visible. Requires a high-clearance vehicle and directions.

stops.name: Petrified Forest National Park
stops.blurb: The only national park the highway ran directly through. A line of telephone poles and a rusted Studebaker mark the old roadbed.

stops.name: Painted Desert Inn
stops.blurb: A Pueblo Revival lodge inside Petrified Forest, restored as a museum with Hopi murals. The inn is the reason to leave I-40 for the park road.

stops.name: Joe & Aggie's Cafe
stops.blurb: Family-run since 1943 and still serving the same green chile.

stops.name: Wigwam Motel #6
stops.blurb: Fifteen concrete tepees from 1950, one of three surviving Wigwam Villages. Vintage cars parked between them.

stops.name: Butterfield Stage Company
stops.blurb: Western steakhouse a short walk from the Wigwam Motel. Where people staying in the tepees actually eat.

stops.name: Rainbow Rock Shop
stops.blurb: Home-made concrete dinosaurs in loud colours outside a rock shop. Free from the roadside.

stops.name: Jack Rabbit Trading Post
stops.blurb: Famous for the billboard campaign that counted down for hundreds of miles to a sign reading simply HERE IT IS.

stops.name: Standin' on the Corner Park
stops.blurb: A corner, a statue, a mural with a girl in a flatbed Ford. Built entirely on one line of a 1972 song.

stops.name: Dino Drive-Thru
stops.blurb: A dinosaur you can drive under at the remains of Meteor City. Outdoor, odd, and on the later alignment west of the crater.
stops.caution: Mostly outdoor; hours vary.

stops.name: Meteor Crater
stops.blurb: Nearly a mile across and 550 feet deep. Six miles off the route and worth every one of them.

stops.name: Graffiti Gas Station
stops.blurb: An abandoned station at Two Guns, now a canvas of traveler paint. The rest of the ghost town is unstable — look, don't climb.
stops.caution: Ruins are unstable. Stay off floors and roofs.

stops.name: Twin Arrows Trading Post
stops.blurb: Two giant arrows planted in the ground beside an abandoned cafe. Derelict, restored arrows, no services. Pure atmosphere.

stops.name: Winona
stops.blurb: The line in the song exists mainly because it rhymed. There is a 1911 bridge and very little else, which is the appeal.

stops.name: Galaxy Diner
stops.blurb: Chrome-and-vinyl diner on the Flagstaff stretch serving breakfast all day. Reliable stop before the long run west.

stops.name: Museum Club
stops.blurb: A 1931 log-cabin roadhouse built around living ponderosa pines. Still a honky-tonk.

stops.name: Pine Breeze Inn
stops.blurb: An abandoned motor court in the pines that appeared briefly in Easy Rider.

stops.name: Pete's Route 66 Gas Station Museum
stops.blurb: A restored station museum on Williams's main street, a quieter counterweight to the Grand Canyon traffic two blocks over.

stops.name: Ash Fork
stops.blurb: Calls itself the flagstone capital of the world. Bypassed in 1979 and never recovered; stone yards and a small museum remain.

stops.name: Grand Canyon Caverns
stops.blurb: Dry caverns 210 feet down, with a single hotel suite inside them. Also a Cold War fallout shelter still stocked with supplies.

stops.name: Crookton Road — Longest Stretch
stops.blurb: Roadside sign where the longest unbroken original stretch of Route 66 begins — 158 miles of two-lane to the Colorado River.

stops.name: Angel & Vilma's Route 66 Gift Shop
stops.blurb: The barbershop of the man who campaigned to get Historic Route 66 designated after the interstate bypassed the town.

stops.name: Delgadillo's Snow Cap Drive-In
stops.blurb: Built in 1953 from scrap lumber. The staff have run the same practical jokes on customers for seventy years.

stops.name: John Osterman Shell
stops.blurb: A 1930s Shell on the Hualapai stretch, being brought back from roadside ruin. Not always open, but the canopy is the photograph.
stops.caution: Restoration in progress — exterior often the whole visit.

stops.name: Truxton
stops.blurb: Founded in the 1950s to serve the highway and hollowed out by Interstate 40 twenty years later. A motel sign and a garage survive.

stops.name: Keepers of the Wild Nature Park
stops.blurb: Rescue sanctuary for tigers, bears, and wolves in a desert canyon on the loneliest stretch of 66 between Seligman and Kingman.
stops.caution: Closed Tuesdays. Safari tours book ahead.

stops.name: Giganticus Headicus
stops.blurb: A fourteen-foot green head made of chicken wire and papier-mâché, beside a former trading post.

stops.name: Hackberry General Store
stops.blurb: A 1934 store buried in memorabilia and rusting cars, with a red Corvette permanently parked out front.

stops.name: Powerhouse Visitor Center
stops.blurb: A 1907 power station converted to the Route 66 Museum. Good place to get advice before the Oatman climb.

stops.name: Cool Springs Station
stops.blurb: Rebuilt from a ruin on the climb toward Sitgreaves Pass. Stone piers, a small shop, and a serious view.

stops.name: Sitgreaves Pass
stops.blurb: 3,550 feet of switchbacks with no guardrail. Early cars had to reverse up it because gravity-fed fuel wouldn't reach the engine.

stops.name: Gold Road Mine
stops.blurb: A working gold mine on the switchbacks above Oatman that runs underground tours.

stops.name: Oatman
stops.blurb: A former gold-mining town where descendants of prospectors' burros wander the main street and mug traffic for carrots.

stops.name: Old Trails Bridge
stops.blurb: A 1916 steel arch over the Colorado that carried Route 66 until 1948. Now carries a gas pipeline; view only, from the frontage road.

stops.name: Goffs Schoolhouse Museum
stops.blurb: Restored 1914 one-room schoolhouse, later a WWII Army canteen. Volunteer museum at the edge of the Mojave National Preserve.
stops.caution: No regular hours — call ahead.

stops.name: Roy's Motel & Cafe
stops.blurb: A Googie boomerang sign standing alone in the Mojave. The town has one resident population figure and no cell signal.

stops.name: Amboy Crater
stops.blurb: An extinct cinder cone you can hike into. Do it at dawn — there is no shade anywhere.

stops.name: Road Runner's Retreat
stops.blurb: A gutted restaurant and station with its sign still standing in the open desert. No shade, no water, no one.

stops.name: Cadiz Summit
stops.blurb: Concrete shells covered in decades of layered graffiti at the top of a rise. Nothing marks it.

stops.name: Ludlow
stops.blurb: A split town: a working truck stop on the interstate and an abandoned 66-era cafe, motel and garage a few hundred yards north.

stops.name: Bagdad Cafe
stops.blurb: The 1987 film shot here made it a pilgrimage site for European travelers. Still a working cafe in the middle of nowhere.

stops.name: Calico Ghost Town
stops.blurb: An 1881 silver town restored as a county park. Commercial, but the mine tour is real.

stops.name: Route 66 Mother Road Museum
stops.blurb: Inside the restored Casa del Desierto Harvey House railway depot. The building outshines the collection.

stops.name: California Route 66 Museum
stops.blurb: Volunteer-run, in the old Red Rooster Cafe. Strong on the Mojave stretch specifically.

stops.name: Emma Jean's Holland Burger Cafe
stops.blurb: Open since 1947, tiny, and still primarily a place where local tradesmen eat breakfast.

stops.name: Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch
stops.blurb: A forest of welded metal poles hung with hundreds of coloured glass bottles. Free, unstaffed, best in low sun.

stops.name: Wigwam Motel
stops.blurb: The western Wigwam Village, 1949. Restored and operating; the pool is original.

stops.name: Original McDonald's Site & Museum
stops.blurb: The lot where the first McDonald's stood, now an unofficial museum run independently of the company.

stops.name: Mitla Cafe
stops.blurb: Opened 1937, still family-run. The oldest Mexican restaurant on 66, a few blocks from the original McDonald's kiosk. Chile on everything.

stops.name: Sycamore Inn
stops.blurb: A stagecoach stop site dating to the 1840s, rebuilt in 1921, on the old road under mature trees.

stops.name: Magic Lamp Inn
stops.blurb: A 1955 restaurant with a neon lamp sign and an interior essentially unchanged.

stops.name: Cucamonga Service Station
stops.blurb: A 1915 station restored as a local Route 66 museum, on the National Park Service itinerary. Thursday through Sunday.
stops.caution: Thursday–Sunday, 10–4.

stops.name: Aztec Hotel
stops.blurb: 1925 Mayan Revival hotel, on the National Register, largely shuttered. Exterior detail is extraordinary.

stops.name: Fair Oaks Pharmacy
stops.blurb: A 1915 corner drugstore with a working soda fountain on the Arroyo Seco alignment.

stops.name: Original Western Terminus
stops.blurb: Olympic and Lincoln, where the highway actually ended. An unremarkable intersection with a small plaque, a mile inland from the pier everyone photographs.

stops.name: Santa Monica Pier — End of the Trail
stops.blurb: The ceremonial end. The highway's actual western terminus was at Olympic and Lincoln; the pier sign was put up in 2009.
